title: Strings
summary: A string is a character array, and an edit often copies.

parts.rule: Treat a string as a character array with length n. Indexing a character is O(1). Building a new string by repeated concatenation in an immutable language copies on every step and can reach quadratic time. Prefer a builder or a character buffer when you assemble output in a loop.
parts.why: Phone-screen snippets that "just add characters" blow the time budget once n hits 10^5. Interviewers watch for the hidden copy. Naming immutability and the builder before you type the loop shows you see the cost, not only the API.
parts.example: Build the reverse of "abcd". Naive path in an immutable language: start with out="", then out = "d"+out, then "cd"+out, then "bcd"+out, then "abcd"+out. Each step copies the growing prefix, so total character writes are 1+2+3+4 = 10, which is n(n+1)/2. Better path: allocate a length-4 buffer, write s[3], s[2], s[1], s[0] into slots 0..3, then join once. Character writes are exactly 4. Same result "dcba", linear work. For a sliding check that two strings are anagrams of length 5, count frequencies in one pass over each string into a 26-slot table instead of sorting both into new strings.
parts.use: Use string indexing when the problem is a scan, a two-pointer walk, or a window over characters. Use a builder or list-of-chunks when you assemble output in a loop. Use immutable strings freely for keys and comparisons when you are not rebuilding them repeatedly.
parts.refuse: Refuse repeated concatenation inside a hot loop when the language copies on each + and n is large. Refuse treating a string edit as O(1) without stating whether the runtime mutates in place. Refuse sorting characters into a new string when a frequency table answers the same question in linear time. Refuse ignoring Unicode width if the prompt cares about user-visible length rather than code units.

body:
Rule. Treat a string as a character array with length n. Indexing a character is O(1). Building a new string by repeated concatenation in an immutable language copies on every step and can reach quadratic time. Prefer a builder or a character buffer when you assemble output in a loop.

Why it matters. Phone-screen snippets that "just add characters" blow the time budget once n hits 10^5. Interviewers watch for the hidden copy. Naming immutability and the builder before you type the loop shows you see the cost, not only the API.

Worked example. Build the reverse of "abcd". Naive path in an immutable language: start with out="", then out = "d"+out, then "cd"+out, then "bcd"+out, then "abcd"+out. Each step copies the growing prefix, so total character writes are 1+2+3+4 = 10, which is n(n+1)/2. Better path: allocate a length-4 buffer, write s[3], s[2], s[1], s[0] into slots 0..3, then join once. Character writes are exactly 4. Same result "dcba", linear work. For a sliding check that two strings are anagrams of length 5, count frequencies in one pass over each string into a 26-slot table instead of sorting both into new strings.

When to use. Use string indexing when the problem is a scan, a two-pointer walk, or a window over characters. Use a builder or list-of-chunks when you assemble output in a loop. Use immutable strings freely for keys and comparisons when you are not rebuilding them repeatedly.

When to refuse. Refuse repeated concatenation inside a hot loop when the language copies on each + and n is large. Refuse treating a string edit as O(1) without stating whether the runtime mutates in place. Refuse sorting characters into a new string when a frequency table answers the same question in linear time. Refuse ignoring Unicode width if the prompt cares about user-visible length rather than code units.
